name: Interview Transcription and Speaker Separation
title: Interview Transcription and Speaker Separation
answer: Interview transcription and speaker separation covers converting recorded spoken interviews into text and attributing each utterance to the correct participant. In qualitative and mixed methods research this supports coding, thematic analysis, and cross-case comparison when multiple voices are present in one recording. The scope includes handling overlapping speech, crosstalk, accents, background noise, and turn-taking in one-to-one or group interviews. It also covers the preparation of transcripts for downstream qualitative data analysis software and for audit trails.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Interview transcription and speaker separation covers converting recorded spoken interviews into text and attributing each utterance to the correct participant. In qualitative and mixed methods research this supports coding, thematic analysis, and cross-case comparison when multiple voices are present in one recording. The scope includes handling overlapping speech, crosstalk, accents, background noise, and turn-taking in one-to-one or group interviews. It also covers the preparation of transcripts for downstream qualitative data analysis software and for audit trails.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on recorded audio or video files, typically from interviews, focus groups, or field recordings, processed on local workstations, institutional servers, or cloud transcription services. Speech-to-text models and speaker diarization models are the main computational components, often accessed through application programming interfaces or run locally where data sensitivity requires it. Storage and processing must accommodate long audio files, and researchers often keep the original recording alongside the generated transcript for verification.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The typical workflow begins with audio segmentation and voice activity detection, followed by automatic speech recognition to produce a raw transcript with timestamps. Speaker separation, or diarization, clusters speech segments by voice characteristics so that each speaker is labelled consistently, though the labels are usually generic until a researcher maps them to named participants. Researchers then review and correct the transcript, resolve overlapping speech, and align speaker labels with the interview guide or field notes. In mixed methods work, the corrected transcript becomes the unit of analysis for coding and quantification.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk centre on consent, confidentiality, and data protection, because interview audio often contains personal or sensitive information and may identify participants by voice. Researchers need to ensure participants understand how recordings will be transcribed, whether automated tools are used, and where audio or text is stored or processed. Speaker separation can create a false sense of certainty about who said what, so transcripts should be checked against the recording, and any uncertain attribution should be flagged. Provenance matters: the final transcript should record which tools or models were used, what version, and what manual corrections were made, so the analytic record is auditable.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward more accurate transcription of natural speech, including overlapping talk, non-standard dialects, and multilingual interviews, with less manual correction. Speaker separation is improving through models that use both voice characteristics and conversational context, which may reduce errors in group settings. Integration with qualitative analysis software is likely to deepen, allowing researchers to move from audio to coded transcript with clearer links between speaker, utterance, and analytic memo. The main open challenge is maintaining researcher judgement and participant privacy as automation handles more of the transcription and attribution.
